en: Achalbars, which Chubak took,
The very last of the swords,
Arkesken, which Syrgak took—
I knew you would come, my orphan.
As a final bequest, poor man,
I kept thinking, “When he comes, he will take them.”
These are entrusted to us;
I will give them to you; take them away.
Then Manas the leopard,
Making Akkula prance,
The enemy who faced him—
He made those who met him crawl.
Those he faced fled in fear;
Those who fought him did not get far.
If an enemy came out to fight,
He took him in his jaws and chewed him.
No one remained to face him.
At the waist of the lion hero,
Bozkise, which he girded on,
Of fierce Manas alone,
Was the belt that befriended his very soul.
No mortal could bear it in his hands,
Nor dare to take hold of it.
No one apart from Manas
Could endure fastening it at his waist.
I will tell you, my orphan:
At this time it is kept safe
In Khan Kobosh's hands.
That same Bozkise,
Take it away as a gift,
Saying, “It was left by my valiant father,”
And fasten it about your waist.
Akolpok, from your father Manas—
Let me tell you its story.
Its collar gold, its sleeves copper,
Double mail with lark-eye links,
A rich outer coat, a roomy vest,
Bulletproof when worn into battle.
Your valiant mother Kanykey
Orenburg and Margilan—
She had the lands between them searched.
The fiber from there—
She had the merchants beaten
And had it taken by force.
The fiber for its weft
She had strong men twist.
Steel and the finest steel
She had poured into its middle,
And let it settle, dish after dish.
She lined its inside with fine fabric,
Had nine buttons fastened to it.
Your precious mother Kanykey
Worked it with her teeth for seven years without rest.
Keeping her eyes upon that coat,
Her dear eyes grew strained.
From the effort of biting,
Her door-like teeth wore away.
She had a precious weft laid in.
When he entered combat with the enemy,
It satisfied a man's heart.
Arrows could not reach him,
A spear's point could not pass through,
A gun's bullet could not enter.
Akolpok, worn by the king—
When Manas, my caravan, was still here,
When the mighty champions were alive,
With a cotton sash and broad boots,
Kalcha, khan of the Kalmyks—
When they took horses from Keng-Shor,
Ten thousand livestock gathered as tribute,
Countless great beasts of the treasury,
When they raided and took them all,
Their frisking foals—
When they slaughtered them in the water,
Their neighing mares—
When they drove them off without their foals,
Azhybay's Kartkurong,
When it took the lead of the herd,
Their teeming khans—
When they brought them to a day of ruin,
The people who tended the horses—
When they slaughtered them all,
When they raided the horses and fled,
The massed Chinese and Kongurbay,
The people of forty khans gathered
And caught up behind them.
A great and terrible slaughter
Was then taking place.
Against Almambet and Syrgak,
All the unbelieving people surged,
About to wreak havoc,
Almambet and Syrgak—
About to bind and take them alive.
The lion Manas, the fierce hero,
Among the teeming Chinese and Kalmyks
Threw himself into the fray.
Drenched in bloody gore,
They fought on without fleeing;
A great slaughter took place.
Your father Manas, the generous lion,
That guileless, hapless hero,
His wineskin-like nose flaring,
Loomed forward upon Aibanboz.
Aibanboz beneath him,
That beast fit for slaughter, that year
Had reached his forty-fourth year.
The place where they were fighting,
That desert forty days across—
Your leopard father Manas
Was locked in destruction there.
They called it the desert of It-Baspas;
Any mortal caught there
Had to think of death.
When a swan flew there, its ears
Were burned by that place.
When a wild ass passed, its hooves
Were burned by that desert.
There was not a pinch of grass to eat;
Day and night in that place,
They fought with mounting fury,
Drenched in bright red blood,
Battling long without respite.
While the slaughter raged,
Kongurbay, the skilled judge,
Knew Aibanboz would cease to move,
And hero Kalcha knew it plainly.
Khan Manas's Aibanboz,
His long ears flapping,
When he had gone six days without water,
Would not move, though he struggled.
If pulled uphill, Aibanboz,
His bowels and belly jolted.
If pulled downhill, that pig's
Pit-like groin rumbled.
In such a state, Aibanboz,
When he would no longer move,
Six thousand Chinese and countless officials,
Kongurbay their elder,
And beside Kongurbay,
Skilled spearmen,
And mighty wielders of battle-axes,
With bead plumes and coral stones,
Their chief ruler mingled among them,
His armored arm-guards spreading wide.
All their officials were there;
Their resourceful Khan Kalcha was there.
Then they charged in fiercely
At the outstanding hero, fierce Manas.
“My men in iron-cord mail,
All my dagger-handed warriors,
The hero Manas is a mighty man,
A lion of extraordinary strength.
Let us capture him alive,
To the Old Khan of Beijing
Let us take him as a gift.
For the treasury's forty whores,
Let us go and make him a stallion.
If a male child is born from him,
Without shame or wounded pride,
Let us put a golden crown upon him,
Seat him on a golden throne,
And raise him up as khan.”
Khan Kongurbay said this,
And the massed Chinese, the khagan's people,
Surged in and thrust their spears.
Khan Kongurbay and Ylama
Went in without sparing their lives.
Even if seventy spears struck at once,
Its sleeves did not wear through.
Even if sixty spears struck at once,
Its weft did not wear through.
Your leopard father Manas—
Akolpok, which he chose to wear,
Bulletproof when he entered combat,
Akolpok, which he cherished—
We kept it deliberately,
So my dear orphan might wear it.
I kept it in trust;
Know this service I have done.
Saying, “My uncles gave me a gift,”
Wear it away, my dear orphan.
Your father the khan's Akkelte—
Let me tell you its story.
Of supremely keen iron, apple-headed,
It makes no distinction between far and near.
A support left by your father,
It is property for you to shoot.
Your Akkelte is ready; take it away.
And now, my only one, hear my words.
Narbuurul, left by your father—
When your father Manas died,
Buurul observed mourning.
Tethered, he would not stand still;
Released, he would not graze.
Neighing and shaking his head,
Distressed and bewildered,
Though an animal, that wondrous creature
Cried aloud in mourning.
His forelock thinned upon his crown;
Tears poured from his eyes.
Bellowing without cease,
His desire, in this way,
Buurul had attained.
With seven thousand coursers following,
Buurul departed.
Unseen by a single person,
Letting no one catch him,
He stopped upon the mountaintop,
And grazed upon nine hills.
He grazed where there were no people,
Drank water in deserted places.
From that day to this,
He cannot be caught by the eye.
He has vanished into the unseen;
No one knows where he is.
There is no one who says, “I saw him”;
No mortal who says, “I know.”
My support in life, left by Manas,
My mirror, left by my khan!
When your father Manas was here,
Six multitudes of horses upon the hills,
Coursers and swift steeds mingled,
Increased and did not diminish.
The keen steel left by your father
Has grown finer, never chipped.
The treasure left by your father
Has only filled, never dwindled.
Here is the livestock your father left,
Here are the people your father left,
Here is the treasure your father left,
Here is the property your father left!
Your father Manas, the leopard—
If you come and settle in Talas,
My dear orphan,
This great people standing here
Are the subjects your father left.
Long I wandered in grief and distress,
The orphan of Khan Manas—
I wondered when he would arrive.
Here is the treasury, here the people,
Who pined for you, my orphan—
Here am I, your uncle Abyke!
Abyke, the wise kinsman,
To the child who came from afar
Now gave his counsel earnestly;
The orphan who came from afar
He greeted, standing there in tears.
What Abyke had said—
Let us leave that aside for now,
In Akylay's embrace,
He had lain for days and nights—
Let us begin to tell of Kobosh:
Foolish and envious,
Among the six was Kobosh, born to wickedness.
The swine was truly worse than most.
